text: Why can the model itself not be the security boundary against indirect prompt injection?
solutions: Models are too slow to check every instruction
Instructions and data reach the model through the same channel, so it cannot reliably tell them apart
Models never read tool descriptions
MCP encrypts tool descriptions so the model cannot inspect them

text: In this lesson, where did the injected instruction come from?
solutions: The prompt the learner typed
The sample.csv invoice file
The tool metadata published by the MCP server
The WebGoat login page

text: Which control stopped the token from being accepted even when the assistant followed the injected instruction?
solutions: A deterministic server-side check that refuses credentials in tool arguments
A system prompt that asks the model to be careful
Switching to a larger model
A prompt injection detector that scores each tool description

text: A repository you cloned contains a .mcp.json file that points at a server you do not know. What should happen?
solutions: Load it automatically, project configuration is trusted
Load it and enable auto-approve so the task runs faster
Nothing, MCP configuration cannot affect the assistant
Treat it as untrusted input: review the server and approve it explicitly before the client loads it

text: What should a tool-call confirmation prompt show to protect the user?
solutions: A short summary of the call written by the model
The real tool name and the full argument values that will be sent
Only the name of the MCP server
Nothing, one approval per session is enough
